decisions.reason: The City publishes automated bicycle-counter data, so readers would learn whether the counters recorded nearly 1.3 million trips in that period.
City traffic counts and before-and-after corridor studies can show whether bike-lane projects increased, reduced, or did not change vehicle delays. The two readers split GO and PARK.
City project plans and roadway drawings can identify where vehicle lanes were converted to bike lanes and whether this happened across the city.
Household travel surveys and bicycle counters can show how many trips are made by bike and how heavily the lanes are used.
Statistics Canada commuting tables and the regional household travel survey can directly check whether bicycles account for about 2 percent of trips.
The City's approved capital budget states the spending period, so readers would learn whether the $100 million covers one year or four.
The capital budget can show which projects belong in each total and whether active transportation represents about 1 percent of comparable road spending.
The City's project budget and construction limits can directly check the stated cost and 600-metre length.
Administration's report, the motions and Council's recorded votes can show what review was recommended and whether Council rejected it.
Because this proposition attributes a specific decision to an identifiable person, the site's lack of a right-of-reply process rules out a panel.

The two readers split on this one. Route reports and engagement records can show which data the City used, whom it consulted and how affected residents were notified. Against that: This site does not adjudicate allegations against named individuals regarding their personal communication with residents. It waits rather than being dropped.
Petitions and hearing submissions cannot establish what most affected residents or Edmontonians think; reopen this when a representative neighbourhood and citywide survey is available.

The two readers split on this one. The City publishes official voter turnout statistics for municipal elections. Against that: Both wordings already put turnout below 40 percent, leaving only a routine calculation from the official election result that no argument here disputes. It waits rather than being dropped.
Council's published compensation policy can show whether councillors receive a vehicle allowance and its amount.
City budgets and provincial tax records can show how Edmonton roads are funded and whether fuel taxes or registration fees flow to the City for that purpose.
City design standards, approval records and signed drawings can show what professional engineering review bike routes receive before construction.
The City's cycling inventory and road-classification data can be matched to calculate the facility types and identify any routes on arterial roads.
City project maps and provincial road classification records can confirm the location and designation of this roadway. The two readers split GO and PARK.

The route's age is documented, but the City does not publish a complete complaint history; reopen this if route-level 311 and correspondence records become available. The two readers split NO and PARK.

The two readers split on this one. Year-round counter and travel-survey data can show how sharply cycling falls in winter and whether meaningful everyday use persists. Against that: Whether something is 'unworkable' is a subjective judgement, not a factual proposition. It waits rather than being dropped.
Several years of winter counter data can show whether cold-season ridership is increasing, including during severe cold periods.
The City's snow-clearing priorities and operational records can show whether bike lanes are scheduled or cleared ahead of adjacent streets.
The City's operating budget can show the annual amount assigned to maintaining the cycling network.

The two readers split on this one. City bike network maps show whether there is a dedicated bike lane on Whyte Avenue. Against that: The City's cycling map settles this as a simple street-name correction, not a disputed proposition that warrants a panel. It waits rather than being dropped.
Route drawings and parking inventories can show how many on-street spaces each project removes and where replacement access is provided.
The approved capital budget and Council vote can show the amount, purpose and schedule of the bike-network expansion.

The two readers split on this one. City Council meeting minutes record the motions introduced by councillors and how they were voted on. Against that: Because this proposition attributes specific actions to identifiable people, the site's lack of a right-of-reply process rules out a panel. It waits rather than being dropped.
City Council voting records can show if a consistent group of seven councillors votes together on active transportation issues. The two readers split GO and PARK.
City project updates and school board communications can confirm if the plan was stopped and the reasons given. The two readers split GO and PARK.
The project plan can check the access change, but the City needs route-level counts before the claim of one rider a week can be tested.
Fire Rescue Services and EMS response time data and operational reports document any delays caused by road infrastructure. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Emergency-service procedures and protected-lane design standards can show whether responders are permitted and able to use the lanes to bypass queues.
City design standards and DATS operational reports indicate whether bike lane barriers restrict accessible loading. The two readers split GO and PARK.
City accessibility standards and design drawings can show whether protected lanes provide wheelchair travel and accessible-van loading space.
The City's road-classification map and corridor plans can show whether that part of 50th Street functions as a collector or an arterial.

The two readers split on this one. The City publishes salary ranges for its administrative and management positions. Against that: Pay records could show individual salaries, but those amounts would not test the source's argument about whether the bike-lane policy is justified. It waits rather than being dropped.
There is no public record or automated counter that tracks the specific number of cyclists arriving at Heritage Days in a given hour. The two readers split NO and PARK.
Bylaw ticket data shows whether enforcement actions are taken against cycling on sidewalks. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Provincial legislation, ministerial orders and official correspondence can show whether Edmonton was directed to stop construction or remove arterial-road lanes.
Provincial legislation and official communications to municipalities are public records. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Election results record votes, not what voters knew or intended when casting them, so no public record can settle this proposition.
Provincial legislation outlines the rules and timelines for municipal recall petitions, and active petitions are registered publicly. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Transit schedules and traffic data can be compared to determine travel times for regional commutes. The two readers split GO and PARK.
City budget documents show how much the active transportation budget contributes to the overall property tax levy. The two readers split GO and PARK.
City procurement records and project accounts can show which route designs have been paid for and which construction contracts have been signed.
Archived design standards and completed project drawings can show whether Edmonton progressed through the three stated forms of bike-lane construction.
Current and historical cycling maps can identify dead ends and missing links, including gaps beside the LRT.
Business closures are observable, but reopen this when customer-access or business data can link those closures to transportation access rather than other causes.
Collision records, route designs and before-and-after user surveys can show whether protected routes reduce injuries and make families more willing to ride.
Before-and-after collision data can show whether bike lanes and street-lab changes produced measurable safety benefits for cyclists and pedestrians.
There is no systematic public record or dataset capturing the frequency of harassment incidents that do not result in a collision or police report. The two readers split NO and PARK.
Budgets, infrastructure-condition reports and service results can compare bike-lane spending with the documented deficits in roads, alleys and seasonal maintenance.

The two readers split on this one. City engineering plans show the configuration of bike lanes on 132 Avenue. Against that: Project records can confirm that lanes were installed, but whether they wrecked the street is an opinion no public record can settle. It waits rather than being dropped.

The two readers split on this one. Tax and budget records can test the factual premise by showing how much municipal-road funding comes from drivers' fuel taxes and registration payments. Against that: Whether cyclists should be registered is a policy opinion, not a factual proposition. It waits rather than being dropped.
Road classifications, traffic counts and school-access studies can show 79 Street's role in diverting traffic from 75 Street and serving school trips.
No removal project has been specified, so reopen this when Council approves a cancellation and the City publishes a removal estimate. The two readers split NO and PARK.
Terms such as "barely functions" and the demand to finish one project before another are value judgements that a public record cannot settle.
LRT schedules, operating-speed reports and collision records can compare its speed with ordinary cycling and count deaths by year.
The hearing register may disclose organizational affiliations, but reopen the payment claim only if speakers or sponsoring groups publish funding records.
The hearing's speaker list and recorded positions can directly show how many registered or spoke for and against the proposal.
City and provincial capital budgets can total Edmonton road projects and show whether spending, including the Yellowhead program, reaches billions.

The two readers split on this one. The budgets for both the 50th Street project and the four-year active transportation plan are public records. Against that: Once the two stated costs are accepted, "nearly double" is settled arithmetic rather than a separate factual question. It waits rather than being dropped.
Statistics Canada census data cross-references commuting modes with income and education levels. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Travel surveys typically collect data on whether individuals use multiple modes of transportation, including both cycling and driving. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Municipal taxes fund shared services regardless of each resident's personal use, a basic feature of taxation that nobody in this argument meaningfully disputes.
The general benefits are researchable, but an Edmonton panel needs local travel-access and health data that can be linked to cycling-infrastructure use. The two readers split NO and PARK.
Project reports can show why each road was narrowed and whether combining traffic calming with a bike lane reduced the project's cost.

The two readers split on this one. City traffic bylaws and neighborhood road design maps list the speed limits and configurations of specific streets. Against that: The speed limit and layout on one street are simple map and sign lookups on which no argument in this source depends. It waits rather than being dropped.
Procurement schedules and tender records can show whether the routes could still enter construction during the 2026 season.
Council records and signed municipal agreements can show whether Edmonton formally committed itself to becoming a 15-minute city.
Edmonton's zoning bylaw can directly show whether developments remain subject to minimum parking requirements.
The site has no right-of-reply process for a proposition alleging a personal motive involving an identifiable person.

The two readers split on this one. City project records show whether the bike lane on 189 Street was removed and at what cost. Against that: Because this proposition attributes a costly past action to an identifiable person, the site's lack of a right-of-reply process rules out a panel. It waits rather than being dropped.
The hearing agenda, procedural ruling and speaker queue can show whether time was cut from five minutes to three and whether 70 speakers were waiting.
Budget amendments and Council votes can show whether money assigned to the recreation centre was redirected to the bike network.

The two readers split on this one. City Council reports and agendas show the details of snow removal proposals and their budget implications. Against that: The number and cost of snow-removal proposals are side details, and no argument in this source depends on whether Administration presented exactly two. It waits rather than being dropped.

The two readers split on this one. The City Council and committee meeting agendas list upcoming items for debate. Against that: A possible future calcium-chloride debate does not support or challenge any argument in this source about the bike-lane decision. It waits rather than being dropped.
School locations and the route plan can directly show how many schools are on the affected part of 132 Avenue.

The two readers split on this one. The City's capital budget and project reports document the cost of streetlight replacement programs. Against that: Saying that new infrastructure costs taxpayers something is a truism, and the proposition gives no amount or disputed consequence to check. It waits rather than being dropped.
Historical ETS route maps and service-change reports can show which community bus routes were removed and when.
Official transportation plans, bylaws and Council reports can show whether a year-round downtown car ban is planned.
Official decisions from Canadian municipalities can show which cities have ordered bike-lane removals and how broad those removals are.

The two readers split on this one. Provincial traffic law can show where cyclists may legally ride when no bike lane is available. Against that: This is a statement of basic traffic law that no one disputes. It waits rather than being dropped.
Individual anecdotes cannot establish the pattern; reopen this when a public census table links Edmonton commuting mode with occupation.

The two readers split on this one. City parking costs, maintenance spending and foregone meter revenue can show what taxpayers provide when curb parking is free to the driver. Against that: This is an economic argument about definitions rather than a factual proposition settled by a record. It waits rather than being dropped.
Because this proposition concerns the personal conduct of identifiable officeholders, the site's lack of a right-of-reply process rules out a panel.
City permit data and urban canopy reports show the number of trees removed and parking spots affected by infill developments. The two readers split GO and PARK.
City flood mitigation reports and EPCOR claims data quantify the cost of drainage-related property damage. The two readers split GO and PARK.
Reopen this when snow-clearing records, usable road-width measurements and winter collision data can be linked for Whyte Avenue. The two readers split NO and PARK.
Police collision data with coded contributing factors can show what share of reported bicycle collisions was attributed to cyclists.
City road design standards specify lane widths and clearance requirements for passing stopped vehicles safely. The two readers split GO and PARK.
The location is missing and causation requires pavement-condition and traffic-load records for that road before and after the lane change.
The regional household travel survey can show bicycle trips by purpose and distance, including the shares made for commuting and recreation.
City engineering drawings specify whether the curb lines are being moved to accommodate the bike lanes. The two readers split GO and PARK.
That roads carry service, freight and emergency vehicles is an undisputed truism rather than a proposition that needs a panel.
A review of the City's project pages and linked records can show whether one public location contains the costs, studies, assessments and engagement results.

The two readers split on this one. Connectivity studies and before-and-after mode-share data can test the factual premise that completing safe links leads more people to cycle instead of drive. Against that: This is a policy opinion and a prediction, not a factual proposition. It waits rather than being dropped.
The general capacity advantage of mass transit over individual cars is settled arithmetic and does not decide the bike-lane argument in this source.

The two readers split on this one. Census housing and population data, together with City servicing-cost reports, can show how growth and low-density expansion affect Edmonton's finances. Against that: Whether continued sprawl is 'unsustainable' is a policy argument, not a factual proposition. It waits rather than being dropped.
